app_summary: An online shop selling astronomy products, based on the OpenTelemetry Demo. final_report.root_cause: The latency was caused by internal queuing/processing inside the single frontend-proxy (Envoy) instance. Envoy was accepting/holding requests and spending multiple seconds processing them (observed as many frontend-proxy-only multi-second traces), likely exacerbated by increased traffic and a missing global downstream connection limit (warning present in logs). The ~10s traces that point to image-provider are not caused by image-provider CPU/IO work or downstream dependencies; they reflect time spent waiting in the proxy/network/client path and/or tracing timestamp/instrumentation issues (image-provider spans show negative/zero durations), not slow internal work in image-provider. A separate configuration misalignment exists (image-provider Service port name "tcp-service" vs Pod containerPort name "service") but numeric ports match and this is a secondary misconfiguration, not the primary cause of the observed tail latency.
affected_resources: Kubernetes Service object: image-provider (port name mismatch: Service.name="tcp-service" vs Pod.containerPort.name="service")
Envoy configuration: missing global downstream connection limit (envoy.resource_monitors.global_downstream_max_connections)
final_report.evidence_summary: Priority-1 checks: image-provider pod is Running, Ready, low CPU, stable threads, low memory, no restarts or OOMs (rules out pod-level resource exhaustion). Priority-2: frontend-proxy calls image-provider on numeric port 8081; Service and Pod numeric ports match but port names differ (tcp-service vs service) — a misconfiguration but not blocking. Priority-3: traces show many frontend-proxy-only requests with multi-second durations; frontend-proxy logs contain a warning about no global downstream connection limit; only a single frontend-proxy pod is running — all pointing to internal Envoy queuing/processing as the source of 2–4s tail latency. Priority-4: traces that implicate image-provider show client and Envoy spans with ~10s durations while the image-provider server span is zero/negative-duration (sanitized), indicating timestamp/instrumentation skew or that the time was spent waiting in the proxy/network rather than image-provider processing. Network transmit/receive spikes on image-provider pod correlate to elevated traffic/large payload transfers but CPU/IO are low. Priority-5 dependency checks returned no downstream calls from image-provider, supporting that image-provider is not blocked on external services. Service endpoint mapping is correct (Endpoints: 10.244.1.13:8081).
final_report.investigation_summary: Investigations prioritized higher-weight tasks first. Priority-1 (pod resource checks) disproved CPU/memory/threads/restart causes for image-provider. Priority-2 confirmed the frontend-to-image numeric port wiring is correct but discovered a port name mismatch on the image-provider Service (non-blocking in this case). Priority-3 focused on frontend-proxy and found frontend-only multi-second traces, a single frontend-proxy pod, and a log warning about missing global_downstream_max_connections; metrics did not show resource exhaustion. Priority-4 trace-level analysis showed client and proxy spans capturing long wall-clock wait times while image-provider spans were zero/negative-duration (instrumentation/timestamp issue). Priority-5 dependency discovery returned no downstream services for image-provider. Correlating prioritized findings yields a causal chain: elevated traffic/large transfers + single Envoy instance + missing global downstream connection limit (and/or an internal HTTP filter/buffering behavior) → Envoy internal queuing/processing → multi-second tail latency at frontend-proxy; image-provider appears slow in traces due to proxy waiting and span timestamp artifacts rather than actual service processing delays. The image-provider Service port-name mismatch is a separate misconfiguration to fix but did not cause the incident.
